clue.text: Robbie Burns, say, in his cottage

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the words his cottage, running across the word break

explanation.surface: The poet Robert Burns pictured at home in his humble cottage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals letters lodged inside 'his cottage', across the gap between the words. Burns was Scotland's national poet, so 'say' marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns was born in Ayrshire, making him an example of a native of Scotland.

clue.text: One madame stifling a Parisian male — not susceptible

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: stifling means smothering, so one piece is wrapped around the other here

parts.note: Mme is the standard abbreviation for the French title madame
a Parisian would say un for 'a' before a masculine noun

explanation.surface: A Frenchwoman muffling a man, immune to his charms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stifling' signals the container; 'a Parisian male' is French 'a' in its masculine form, a nod to the French title beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone immune to an infection or influence is protected from it, not open to catching it.

clue.text: Noticed fan becoming odd, someone getting close and personal?

indicators.note: becoming odd means turning strange, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

explanation.walkthrough: 'becoming odd' rearranges the letters of NOTICED FAN. The question mark admits the definition is a playful description.
explanation.definitionFit: A trusted friend you share secrets with is someone with whom you are intimate and personal.

clue.text: Nineteenth-century PM's a revolutionary without feeling

indicators.note: revolutionary here means turning round, so the pieces before it are read backwards

parts.note: Sir Robert Peel was British Prime Minister in the 1830s and 1840s; with the 's he gives PEELS

explanation.surface: A Victorian prime minister cast as a heartless revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' turns PEELS + A round, making the whole word backwards. Robert Peel founded London's police, hence 'bobbies'.
explanation.definitionFit: A limb that has gone to sleep is numb, having lost all sensation.

clue.text: What may be procured from manufacturer

indicators.note: may be suggests the letters can become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking what goods might be obtained from a factory owner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' signals that PROCURED can be rearranged; 'What' and 'from' just link it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm that makes goods is a maker or producer of them, the same idea in other words.

clue.text: Game seen in photograph

definitions.meaning: a children's card game where players shout when two matching cards appear
a snapshot, a quick informal picture

explanation.surface: A sporting fixture captured in a press picture.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a matching card game and an informal photograph taken quickly.

clue.text: Sort of delivery man said to fall down when fatigued?

indicators.note: said means spoken, so we want a word that sounds like the clue's word

parts.note: a man is a male
to drop is to collapse from exhaustion, as in 'shop till you drop'

explanation.surface: A tired postman so exhausted he might collapse on his round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' makes a sound-alike of the word for a man; 'fall down when fatigued?' is the phrase 'drop from exhaustion'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mail drop is a place where letters are left for collection, a kind of delivery arrangement.

clue.text: Boring landlord's rule no longer taken notice of?

parts.note: something boring is dead, lifeless and dull
a landlord lets property, so is jokingly a letter

explanation.walkthrough: LETTER is read as 'one who lets'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead letter is a law still on the books but no longer enforced or obeyed.

clue.text: Groom wanting old band

parts.note: to groom hair is to comb it

explanation.surface: A bridegroom missing his former band.
explanation.definitionFit: A combo is a small group of jazz or pop musicians.

clue.text: Set of beliefs Indian abandoned finally

clue.text: Driver wanting tea always, highly amusing person coming in

explanation.walkthrough: 'coming in' signals the insertion; 'wanting' is only a link word, not a deletion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A charioteer drives a chariot, so is a driver of a horse-drawn vehicle.

clue.text: Char spoke out, a nag getting much put upon?

definitions.text: a nag getting much put upon?

explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges the letters of CHAR SPOKE. A 'char' is a British cleaning woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A packhorse carries loads on its back, so is a horse with much put upon it.

clue.text: The man given an opening to collect foreign money — it's providential

an gives the article A

indicators.note: to collect means to gather in, so one piece holds another

parts.note: a vent is an opening

explanation.walkthrough: 'to collect' signals the container; the sen is a hundredth of a yen, among other currencies.
explanation.definitionFit: Something heaven-sent arrives as if by divine favour, perfectly timed and lucky.

clue.text: Most up-to-date home you and I would settle in

clue.text: England's opener, one looking embarrassed about getting a duck
